screens.title: Complete the Words: Honeybee dances
text: Honeybees share information about food in a surprising way. When a {{r11a1}} finds a {{r11a2}} patch {{r11a3}} flowers, {{r11a4}} returns {{r11a5}} the {{r11a6}} and {{r11a7}} a {{r11a8}} dance {{r11a9}} the {{r11a10}} of the comb. The angle of the dance shows the direction of the food relative to the sun, and the length of the waggling run tells other bees how far they must fly. Researchers have found that bees can follow these signals even when the sun is hidden by clouds. This system allows a colony to send many workers to the best flowers within a few hours.

screens.title: Complete the Words: Sleep and memory
text: Sleep does much more than help the body rest. During {{r11b1}} sleep, {{r11b2}} brain {{r11b3}} the {{r11b4}} of {{r11b5}} day {{r11b6}} moves {{r11b7}} information {{r11b8}} long-term {{r11b9}}. In {{r11b10}} well-known study, students who slept after learning a list of words remembered more of them the next morning than students who stayed awake. Scientists believe that the sleeping brain also removes weaker connections, which makes useful memories easier to find later. For this reason, staying up all night before an exam may actually harm performance.

screens.title: Campus Bike Repair Day
text: Campus Bike Repair Day

Saturday, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., outside the Student Center. Volunteer mechanics will check brakes, adjust gears and fix flat tires at no cost. Replacement parts such as chains and lights are available at cost price. Bikes must be dropped off before noon to be ready the same day. Please remove baskets and child seats before you arrive.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To announce a free service for keeping bicycles in good condition
To sell new bicycles to students at a discount
To recruit volunteer mechanics for the Student Center
To explain new parking rules for bicycles on campus

why.en: Main purpose (paraphrase): free repair service. B and C reuse words from the text (bikes, volunteer mechanics, Student Center) but distort the meaning.
why.tr: Ana amaç (parafraz): ücretsiz bakım hizmeti. B/C metindeki kelimeleri (bikes, volunteer mechanics, Student Center) kullanıp anlamı bozuyor.

questions.stem: What will most likely happen to a bike that is dropped off at 1 p.m.?
options: It may not be ready until a later day.
It will be checked by mechanics at no cost.
Its basket will be removed by the volunteers.
It will receive new parts at cost price.

why.en: Inference: a bike not dropped off before noon will not be ready the same day. B is true but does not answer the question.
why.tr: Çıkarım: öğleden önce bırakılmayan bisiklet aynı gün hazır olmaz. B doğru bir bilgi ama soruyu yanıtlamıyor.

screens.title: Hiking Club: change of plans
text:
From: Lena Ortiz (Hiking Club)
Subject: Change of plans for Sunday

Hi everyone, the weather service has issued a storm warning for the mountains this weekend, so we are moving Sunday's hike to the following Saturday. The bus will leave from the same place, but one hour earlier, at 7 a.m., because the new trail is longer. If you can no longer join, please reply by Thursday so we can offer your seat to someone on the waiting list. Those who already paid for the bus do not need to pay again.
— Lena

questions.stem: Why was the hike moved?
options: Dangerous conditions are expected in the area.
The bus company cancelled the Sunday trip.
The mountain trail was closed for repairs.
Too few members signed up for Sunday.

why.en: Paraphrase: "storm warning" → dangerous conditions are expected. The others are not in the text.
why.tr: Parafraz: "storm warning" → tehlikeli koşullar bekleniyor. Diğerleri metinde yok.

questions.stem: How is the new trip different from the original plan?
options: It leaves one hour earlier in the morning.
It leaves from a different place.
It costs more than the first trip.
It follows a shorter trail.

why.en: The change: one hour earlier. B and D say the opposite of the text (same place, longer trail).
why.tr: Fark: bir saat erken. B ve D metnin söylediğinin tersi (same place, longer trail).

questions.stem: What should a member who cannot attend do?
options: Reply by Thursday so the seat can be offered to someone else.
Find a replacement from the waiting list.
Pay for the bus again on Saturday.
Join the original hike on Sunday.

why.en: Detail: "reply by Thursday" → let them know before the deadline. B borrows "waiting list" from the text and puts the responsibility on the member.
why.tr: Detay: "reply by Thursday" → son tarihten önce haber ver. B metindeki "waiting list" kelimesini kullanıp sorumluluğu üyeye yüklüyor.

screens.title: Urban Heat Islands
text: On a summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Scientists call this an urban heat island. The main cause is the material that cities are built from: asphalt, concrete and brick absorb sunlight during the day and slowly release that heat at night.

Cities also lack the natural cooling that plants provide. Trees shade the ground, and they release water vapor through their leaves, which cools the surrounding air in much the same way that sweat cools skin. Where green spaces are replaced by roads and buildings, this effect disappears.

The consequences go beyond discomfort. Warmer nights prevent people from recovering from daytime heat, and heat waves in cities are linked to more hospital visits. Some cities now paint roofs white, plant trees along streets and build parks, and early results suggest that these simple changes can lower local temperatures noticeably.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The causes and effects of extra warmth in urban areas, and possible solutions
The history of the building materials used in large cities
The way sweat helps people stay comfortable in hot weather
Differences in summer weather between countries

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase). B and C mistake details (materials, sweat) for the whole.
why.tr: Ana fikir (parafraz). B ve C metindeki ayrıntıları (materials, sweat) bütün sanıyor.

questions.stem: The word "release" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
options: give off
store up
reflect
block

why.en: Vocabulary in context: release = give off.
why.tr: Bağlamda kelime: release = give off.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention sweat in paragraph 2?
options: To compare the way trees cool the air with how sweat cools skin
To show that people in cities sweat more than people in the countryside
To suggest that hot weather is dangerous for health
To describe how plants take in water from the ground

why.en: Author's purpose: to compare how trees cool the air with a familiar process (sweating). B builds a false claim from words in the text.
why.tr: Yazarın amacı: ağaçların havayı serinletmesini tanıdık bir süreçle (terleme) karşılaştırmak. B metindeki kelimelerle yanlış bir iddia kuruyor.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about people who live in city centers during a heat wave?
options: They get little relief even after the sun goes down.
They visit parks more often than other residents.
They usually paint their roofs white.
They are less affected than people in the countryside.

why.en: Inference: warm nights prevent recovery. C wrongly attributes "paint roofs white" to individuals.
why.tr: Çıkarım: sıcak geceler toparlanmayı engelliyor. C metindeki "paint roofs white" ifadesini kişilere yanlış atfediyor.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, which step have some cities taken?
options: Planting trees along streets
Building roads to replace green spaces
Opening more hospitals during heat waves
Using darker materials on roofs

why.en: Detail: planting trees along streets. B mistakes the cause in paragraph 2 for the solution; D says the opposite.
why.tr: Detay: sokaklara ağaç dikmek. B paragraf 2'deki nedeni çözüm sanıyor; D tersini söylüyor.

hard.title: Complete the Words: Antibiotic resistance
text: Antibiotic resistance is not a new phenomenon, but its acceleration has alarmed public health authorities. Whenever {{r11c1}} are {{r11c2}} to {{r11c3}} antibiotic, {{r11c4}} few {{r11c5}} that {{r11c6}} to {{r11c7}} protective {{r11c8}} survive {{r11c9}} reproduce, {{r11c10}} replacing their vulnerable competitors. Because bacteria can also exchange genetic material directly, resistance that emerges in one species may spread rapidly to entirely unrelated organisms. Consequently, the unnecessary prescription of antibiotics, together with their widespread use in livestock, has substantially reduced the effectiveness of medicines once considered reliable.

hard.title: Library loan policy
text: Main Library — new loan policy

Effective March 1, the main library will replace its fixed loan periods with a demand-based system. Items with no waiting list will renew automatically up to five times, so most borrowers will no longer need to visit the desk. However, once another user places a hold on an item you have borrowed, your loan will be shortened to seven days, and you will receive an email with the new due date. Overdue fines are being abolished; instead, borrowing privileges will be suspended until held items are returned. Laptops and other equipment remain excluded from the new system.

questions.stem: What is the main change described in the notice?
options: How long people keep items will depend on whether others want them
Borrowers must now renew every item at the front desk
The library will begin charging higher fines for late returns
Laptops may now be borrowed for longer periods

why.en: Main change (paraphrase): the loan period depends on demand. B and C contradict the text; D is equipment that is excluded.
why.tr: Ana değişiklik (parafraz): süre talebe bağlı. B ve C metnin tersi; D hariç tutulan ekipman.

questions.stem: What will most likely happen to a student who keeps a requested book past its new due date?
options: The student will be unable to borrow anything else for a while.
The student will pay a fine for each extra day.
The loan will renew automatically up to five times.
The library will send the book to the other user.

why.en: Inference: borrowing rights are suspended instead of a fine. B is the old rule that was removed; C applies to books with no waiting list.
why.tr: Çıkarım: ceza yerine ödünç alma hakkı askıya alınır. B kaldırılan eski kural; C bekleme listesi olmayan kitaplar için.

questions.stem: Which items are NOT covered by the new system?
options: Laptops and other equipment
Items that nobody has requested
Books that are already overdue
Items borrowed before March 1

why.en: Detail/paraphrase: laptops and other equipment → equipment such as computers.
why.tr: Detay/parafraz: laptops and other equipment → bilgisayar gibi ekipman.

hard.title: Color Words and Perception
hard.directions: Read an Academic Passage — upper module
text: Languages differ considerably in how they divide the color spectrum. Russian, for instance, obligatorily distinguishes between lighter blues (goluboy) and darker blues (siniy), whereas English speakers use a single basic term. This raises a question that has long intrigued linguists and psychologists: does the vocabulary a person habitually uses shape the way that person actually perceives the world?

Experimental evidence suggests a modest but measurable influence. In one study, Russian speakers distinguished between two shades of blue more rapidly when the shades straddled the boundary between goluboy and siniy than when both fell within a single category; English speakers showed no comparable advantage. Crucially, the effect vanished when participants simultaneously performed a verbal task that occupied their linguistic resources.

Researchers therefore caution against strong claims. Language does not appear to determine what people are capable of seeing; it seems instead to provide a convenient shortcut that accelerates certain judgments whenever linguistic processing is available.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Color terms can slightly speed up some visual decisions without limiting what people perceive.
Russian speakers are able to see more colors than English speakers can.
Doing a verbal task improves people's ability to tell colors apart.
Linguists disagree about how many basic color terms each language has.

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase). B is too extreme; C contradicts the text.
why.tr: Ana fikir (parafraz). B aşırı uç; C metnin tersi.

questions.stem: The word "straddled" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: crossed
matched
avoided
darkened

why.en: Vocabulary in context: straddle the boundary = fall on both sides of the boundary, cross it.
why.tr: Bağlamda kelime: straddle the boundary = sınırın iki yanına düşmek, sınırı geçmek.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the verbal task?
options: To show that the advantage depends on language being actively engaged
To explain why English speakers performed poorly overall
To prove that Russian speakers have sharper eyesight
To describe a common method of teaching color names

why.en: Author's purpose: the effect disappears when language resources are busy → the advantage depends on actively using language.
why.tr: Yazarın amacı: etki dil kaynakları meşgulken kayboluyor → avantaj dilin aktif kullanımına bağlı.

questions.stem: What would the researchers most likely say about the claim that speakers cannot see a color their language has no word for?
options: It goes further than the evidence supports.
It is confirmed by the Russian study.
It explains why the effect vanished.
It applies only to shades of blue.

why.en: Inference: "caution against strong claims" → it goes beyond the evidence.
why.tr: Çıkarım: "caution against strong claims" → kanıtın ötesine geçiyor.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, when did Russian speakers respond faster?
options: When the two shades fell on different sides of the category boundary
When both shades were dark blue
When they were also doing a verbal task
When English speakers had answered first

why.en: Detail: shades on both sides of the boundary = groups with different names. C contradicts the text.
why.tr: Detay : sınırın iki yanındaki tonlar = farklı adlandırılmış gruplar. C metnin tersi.

easy.title: Complete the Words: School gardens

easy.title: Pool rules
text: Pool Rules
Shower before you swim. Children under 10 must swim with an adult. No running on the pool deck. The pool closes for cleaning every day from 1 to 2 p.m.

questions.stem: What must a parent do if their 8-year-old child wants to swim?
options: Swim with the child in the pool
Leave the child at the front desk
Bring a note from a doctor
Wait until the pool is cleaned

why.en: Detail: "must swim with an adult".

questions.stem: When can people NOT use the pool?
options: During cleaning time, from 1 to 2 p.m.
Early in the morning

easy.title: Why Cats Purr
easy.directions: Read an Academic Passage — lower module
text: Cats purr when they are happy, but that is not the only reason. A cat may also purr when it is hurt, hungry or scared. Mother cats purr to their kittens, and kittens purr back to show that they are fine.

Some scientists think purring helps cats calm down. Others believe the low sound may even help bones and muscles heal faster. Cats make the sound by moving muscles in their throat very quickly as they breathe in and out.
Even after many studies, scientists still do not fully agree on why cats purr.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The different reasons a cat might make a certain sound
How mother cats take care of their kittens
Why cats are happier than other pets
How scientists study the bones of cats

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase).
why.tr: Ana fikir (parafraz).

questions.stem: The word "heal" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: get better
grow longer
move faster
feel colder

why.en: Vocabulary in context: heal = recover.
why.tr: Bağlamda kelime: heal = iyileşmek.

questions.stem: Why do kittens purr back to their mothers?
options: To show their mothers that they are fine
To ask her for more food
To show that they are scared
To help their bones grow

why.en: Detail: "show that they are fine".
why.tr: Detay: "show that they are fine".

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a cat that is purring?
options: It is not always feeling good.
It is always hungry.
It has just finished eating.
It wants to play with people.

why.en: Inference: cats in pain or afraid also purr → purring does not always mean the cat feels good.
why.tr: Çıkarım: acıyan/korkan kedi de mırlar → her zaman iyi hissettiği anlamına gelmez.

questions.stem: How do cats produce the sound?
options: By quickly moving muscles in the throat
By pushing air out through the nose
By tapping their paws on the ground
By closing their mouth very tightly

why.en: Detail.
why.tr: Detay.

intro.en: Listening: Listen and Choose a Response, conversations, announcements and academic talks. Each recording plays once; you may take notes. Speakers use US, British and Australian accents. After the first module the section adapts to you and gets harder or easier.
intro.tr: Listening: Listen and Choose a Response, konuşmalar, duyurular ve akademik konuşmalar. Her ses bir kez çalınır; not alabilirsiniz. Konuşmacılar ABD, İngiliz ve Avustralya aksanlarıyla konuşur. İlk modülden sonra bölüm sana göre zorlaşır ya da kolaylaşır.
intro.es: Listening: Listen and Choose a Response, conversaciones, avisos y clases académicas. Cada grabación se reproduce una vez; puedes tomar notas. Se oyen acentos de EE. UU., Reino Unido y Australia. Después del primer módulo, la sección se adapta a ti y se vuelve más difícil o más fácil.

audio.text: Didn't you say the study group was meeting in the library today?

options: It was, but they moved it to the student center.
Yes, the library closes at nine tonight.
I'd rather not join a new group this term.
No, I haven't been to the library yet.

why.en: A natural reply saying the plan has changed. B repeats "library" but does not answer.
why.tr: Planın değiştiğini söyleyen doğal yanıt. B "library" kelimesini tekrar edip soruyu yanıtlamıyor.

audio.text: Where can I pick up my student ID card?

options: At the registration office on the first floor.
I picked mine up yesterday afternoon.
You'll need a recent photo for that.
It stays valid for four years.

why.en: A "where" question → a place. C is true but does not answer the question.
why.tr: Nerede sorusuna yer. C doğru bir bilgi ama soruyu yanıtlamıyor.

audio.text: How long does the shuttle take to get downtown?

options: About twenty minutes, if traffic is light.
It leaves every half hour from here.
Downtown is really crowded today.
I usually ride my bike there.

why.en: A "how long" question. B gives a frequency (a classic trap).
why.tr: Süre sorusu. B sıklık veriyor (ETS'nin klasik tuzağı).

audio.text: I'm sorry, I can't make it to your presentation tomorrow.

options: No problem, I'll send you the slides.
It starts at ten in room two-oh-four.
I made it all myself, actually.
Tomorrow works better for me too.

why.en: Responding to an apology. C repeats "make it" with a different meaning.
why.tr: Özre karşılık. C "make it" ifadesini yanlış anlamda tekrar ediyor.

audio.text: Would you mind opening the window? It's really warm in here.

options: Sure, let me get that for you.
I don't mind warm weather at all.
The window looks out on the garden.
It was even warmer yesterday.

why.en: Request → agreement. B repeats "mind" and "warm" without answering the request.
why.tr: Rica → kabul. B "mind" ve "warm" kelimelerini tekrar edip isteği yanıtlamıyor.

audio.text: Have you decided which elective to take next term?

options: I'm leaning toward the photography course.
Yes, I decided to take the bus instead.
Next term starts in early September.
The electives are all listed online.

why.en: "Which class" → a choice. D is true but is not an answer.
why.tr: Hangi ders → seçim. D doğru bir bilgi ama yanıt değil.

audio.text: The printer on this floor is out of paper again.

options: There's a box in the supply closet.
I printed my essay last night.
This floor is the quietest one.
Paper is cheaper if you buy it online.

why.en: Problem → solution. B repeats the word "printed".
why.tr: Sorun → çözüm. B "printed" ile kelime tekrarı.

audio.text: Why did the professor cancel today's lecture?

options: She's at a conference in Chicago.
The lecture is in the main hall.
Yes, she cancelled it this morning.
I'll take notes for you next time.

why.en: A "why" question → a reason. C answers a "why" question with "Yes".
why.tr: Neden sorusu → sebep. C "Neden" sorusuna "Evet" diyor.

audio.text: Can I borrow your calculator for the exam?

options: Sorry, I need it myself.
The exam is on Friday morning.
It's a scientific calculator.
I borrowed it from the library.

why.en: Request → refusal with a reason. D repeats "borrow".
why.tr: Rica → ret gerekçesiyle. D "borrow" kelimesini tekrar ediyor.

screens.title: Conversation: At the library
screens.prompt: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.

audio.text: Hi, I'm looking for a book for my history paper, but the catalog says it's checked out.
Let me see. Yes, it's due back next Tuesday. I can put a hold on it for you, and you'll get an email when it's returned.
Next Tuesday? My paper is due on Monday.
In that case, try the electronic version. Most of our history titles are available online, and you can read them from home with your student login.
Oh, I didn't know that. I'll check tonight.

questions.stem: What is the woman's problem?
options: A book she needs is not available right now.
She cannot find the library's online catalog.
She forgot her student login details.
Her paper is due next Tuesday.

why.en: Problem: the book is checked out. D is a wrong detail (Tuesday is when the book is due back).
why.tr: Sorun: kitap ödünçte. D yanlış ayrıntı (Tuesday kitabın dönüş günü).

questions.stem: What will the woman most likely do next?
options: Look for a digital copy of the book
Place a hold on the printed book
Ask her professor for more time
Come back to the library on Tuesday

why.en: Inference: "I'll check tonight" → the electronic version. B was suggested but does not help.
why.tr: Çıkarım: "I'll check tonight" → elektronik sürüm. B önerildi ama işine yaramıyor.

screens.title: Conversation: The career fair
screens.prompt: Listen to a conversation between two students.

audio.text: Are you going to the career fair on Thursday?
I want to, but I have a lab until three, and I heard most companies leave by four.
Actually, they extended the hours this year. It runs until six now, because so many students complained about class conflicts last year.
Really? Then I'll go straight after my lab. Do I need to print my résumé?
Bring a few copies. Some recruiters still prefer paper.

questions.stem: Why did the organizers change the fair's schedule?
options: Many students could not attend because of their classes.
Companies wanted more time to interview students.
The building was not available in the morning.
The woman's lab was moved to Thursday.

why.en: Reason (paraphrase): "class conflicts".
why.tr: Sebep (parafraz): "class conflicts".

questions.stem: What does the man suggest the woman do?
options: Bring printed copies of her résumé
Skip her lab on Thursday
Arrive before the companies leave at four
Email her résumé to the recruiters

why.en: Suggestion: "Bring a few copies". C relies on outdated information.
why.tr: Öneri: "Bring a few copies". C eski bilgiye dayanıyor.

screens.title: Conversation: Office hours
screens.prompt: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.

audio.text: Professor Hale, I wanted to ask about the research project. Could I change my topic?
It's a bit late for that. Proposals were approved two weeks ago. What's the issue?
I planned to interview local farmers, but the harvest has started, and nobody has time to meet.
I see. Rather than changing the topic, why not change the method? You could send a short survey. Farmers can answer it in five minutes whenever they're free.
That could work. I'll draft one this weekend.

questions.stem: Why does the student want to change his topic?
options: The people he planned to talk to are too busy.
His proposal was not approved.
He finished the project two weeks early.
He is no longer interested in farming.

why.en: Reason (paraphrase): harvest → farmers have no time.
why.tr: Sebep (parafraz): hasat → çiftçilerin zamanı yok.

questions.stem: What does the professor imply about the student's topic?
options: It is too late to choose a different one.
It needs more farmers to be useful.
It should focus on the harvest season.
It was the best proposal she received.

why.en: Inference: "It's a bit late for that".
why.tr: Çıkarım: "It's a bit late for that".

screens.title: Announcement: Midterm change
screens.prompt: Listen to an announcement in a classroom.

audio.text: Before you leave, a quick reminder about next week. Because of the holiday on Monday, our midterm exam will move to Wednesday, same time and room. The exam will cover chapters one through six, but not the guest lecture we had last week. You may bring one page of handwritten notes. If you have a conflict with another exam on Wednesday, email me by Friday.

questions.stem: Why is the exam being moved?
options: The original date falls on a holiday.
The room is needed for a guest lecture.
Students asked for more time to study.
The professor will be away on Monday.

why.en: Reason: Monday is a holiday.
why.tr: Sebep: Pazartesi tatil.

questions.stem: What are students allowed to bring to the exam?
options: A sheet of notes written by hand
Their textbooks for chapters one to six
Their notes from the guest lecture
A printed copy of the lecture slides

why.en: Detail (paraphrase): one page of handwritten notes.
why.tr: Detay (parafraz): one page of handwritten notes.

screens.title: Announcement: Lounge kitchen
screens.prompt: Listen to an announcement in a student lounge.

audio.text: Attention, residents. The kitchen in this lounge will be closed tomorrow from nine to noon while the old refrigerator is replaced. Please take any food you've stored in the fridge home with you tonight. Anything left inside will be thrown away by the cleaning staff. The microwave on the second floor will still be available.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
options: To tell residents about a temporary change to a shared space
To advertise a new microwave on the second floor
To ask residents to clean the refrigerator
To invite residents to a cooking event

why.en: Main purpose (paraphrase).
why.tr: Ana amaç (parafraz).

questions.stem: What should residents do tonight?
options: Take their food out of the refrigerator

Tell the cleaning staff about their food

screens.title: Academic Talk: The serial position effect
screens.prompt: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

audio.text: Today I want to talk about something you've probably experienced without realizing it. Imagine I read you a list of twenty words and then ask you to write down as many as you can remember. Most people recall the first few words and the last few words quite well, but the words in the middle tend to disappear. Psychologists call this the serial position effect.

So why does it happen? The words at the beginning get more rehearsal. When you hear the first word, you repeat it to yourself a few times, and that repetition helps move it into long-term memory. By the time the middle of the list arrives, you're trying to rehearse many words at once, so each one gets less attention. The words at the end are a different story. They're still sitting in short-term memory when you start writing, so you can simply read them off, so to speak.

Here's the interesting part. If I make you wait thirty seconds and count backward before you write, the advantage for the final words disappears, but the advantage for the first words remains. That tells us two different memory systems are involved. So, practically speaking, when you study, try not to always start from the same page. Otherwise the middle chapters will always get the least attention.

hard.title: Academic Talk: The wolves of Yellowstone
hard.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an environmental science class.

audio.text: In 1995, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park after an absence of about seventy years. What happened next became one of the most famous stories in ecology. Without wolves, elk had grazed freely along the rivers, eating young willow and aspen trees before they could grow. Once wolves returned, the story goes, elk began avoiding open river valleys where they could easily be hunted. The trees recovered, beavers returned to use the wood, and their dams created ponds that supported fish and birds. Ecologists call a chain of effects like this a trophic cascade.

Now, it's a great story, and parts of it are clearly true. But more recent research suggests the picture is messier. Elk numbers also fell because of hunting by people, harsh winters, and a growing population of bears. And in some areas the willows haven't recovered at all, because without beaver dams the water table had dropped too low for the trees to grow back. In other words, removing a predator can trigger changes that simply adding it back doesn't reverse.
So what's the lesson? Not that the wolves didn't matter. They did. The lesson is that ecosystems don't always work like a light switch. Restoring one species is often only the first step.

questions.stem: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: A well-known ecological success story is more complicated than it first seemed.
Wolves were the only reason the elk population declined.
Beavers are more important to ecosystems than wolves.
Bringing back predators always reverses earlier damage.

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase). B and D are too extreme.
why.tr: Ana fikir (parafraz). B ve D aşırı uç.

questions.stem: Why does the professor mention bears and harsh winters?

To describe dangers that wolves face in the park
To explain why beavers left the rivers
To compare Yellowstone with other national parks

why.en: Purpose.
why.tr: Amaç.

The water table there has returned to normal.

why.en: Inference. D contradicts the talk.

hard.title: Academic Talk: Path dependence
hard.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an economics class.

audio.text: Let's talk about a concept economists call path dependence. The basic idea is that decisions made in the past can limit the choices available today, even when the original reasons no longer apply.

The classic example is the keyboard layout most of you are using right now, known as QWERTY. It was designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters. One popular explanation is that it placed common letter pairs apart so the metal arms wouldn't jam, although historians still argue about how much that really mattered. Either way, the jamming problem disappeared long ago. Other layouts have been designed since then. The Dvorak keyboard, for example, put the most common letters on the middle row, where your fingers already rest, and some people claim it's faster. Yet QWERTY is everywhere.

Why? Because once millions of people had learned it, and schools taught it, and manufacturers produced it, switching became very costly. A new layout would have to be better by enough to make everyone relearn typing at the same time. So the old standard survives, not necessarily because it's the best, but because everyone else is already using it. And economists find the same pattern whenever the value of a choice depends on what everyone else has already chosen.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the lecture?
options: To illustrate an economic idea with a familiar example
To argue that QWERTY is the fastest layout
To explain how mechanical typewriters were built
To recommend that schools teach a new layout

why.en: Purpose (paraphrase).
why.tr: Amaç (parafraz).

questions.stem: What does the professor say about the explanation that QWERTY prevented jamming?
options: Its importance is still debated.
It has been proven completely false.
It explains why QWERTY is faster today.
It was proposed by modern economists.

why.en: Detail (paraphrase): historians still argue.
why.tr: Detay (parafraz): historians still argue.

questions.stem: According to the professor, why has QWERTY survived?

why.en: Reason (paraphrase).

easy.title: Academic Talk: How penguins stay warm
easy.prompt: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.

audio.text: Today we're going to look at how penguins survive in some of the coldest places on Earth. First, they have a thick layer of fat under their skin. This fat works like a blanket and keeps their body heat inside. Second, their feathers are very short and packed tightly together, so cold wind and water can't get through.

Penguins also have a clever trick in their feet. The blood going down to their feet passes right next to the blood coming back up, so heat moves back into the body instead of being lost. Finally, emperor penguins stand together in large groups called huddles. They take turns moving from the cold outside of the group to the warm center. Working together, they can survive temperatures far below freezing.

questions.stem: What is the talk mainly about?
options: The ways penguins protect themselves from the cold
Where penguins find food in winter
How penguins raise their young
Why penguins cannot fly

why.en: Main idea.
why.tr: Ana fikir.

It makes their feathers short.
It stores food for the winter.

why.en: Detail.

options: So that each penguin spends time in the warm center
So that the strongest penguins eat first
So that they can watch for danger
So that young penguins learn to swim

why.en: Reason.
why.tr: Sebep.

questions.stem: Why does the speaker compare fat to a blanket?
options: To help listeners understand how it keeps penguins warm
To show that penguins sleep in groups
To explain why penguins need soft feathers
To describe what penguins build nests with

why.en: Purpose.
why.tr: Amaç.

screens.prompt: Your professor is teaching a class on urban studies. Write a post responding to the professor's question. Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words.

professor.post: Some cities have closed their historic centers to private cars, allowing only pedestrians, bicycles and public transport. Supporters say this makes city centers cleaner and more pleasant; critics argue that it hurts local businesses and makes life harder for residents. Should more cities ban private cars from their historic centers? Why or why not?

students.name: Lin
students.post: Yes. When my hometown closed its old town to cars, the streets became quieter and cafés put tables outside. More people came to walk around, so many shops actually did better than before.

students.name: Daniel
students.post: I disagree. Older people and people with disabilities often rely on cars, and buses don't reach every street. A total ban punishes the people who have the fewest alternatives.
